title: The vow that would not bend
hook: with the Kuru line about to end, Satyavati asks Bhishma to break his vow, and he will not give up truth
carry: satya: a word given is sacred

segments.voice: Yesterday: three princesses from Kashi, Amba let go, and a young king dead without a son. The bride's garland is her choice.

A family line is a thin thread, and Satyavati has watched hers fray to almost nothing. Her husband is gone. Both of her sons by him are gone. Two young widows grieve in the palace. The only grown man of the house is Bhishma, who swore years ago, so her sons would rule, never to take the throne and never to father children. Now she calls him in. The woman his vow made a queen is about to ask him to break it.
screen: `A HUSBAND, TWO SONS, GONE.` → `ONE MAN LEFT.` → `SHE CALLS HIM IN.`

segments.voice: Satyavati makes her case carefully, like someone who has thought about it at night. The offerings to the ancestors, the name of Shantanu, the whole house, she says, now rest on you. You know dharma. Take the throne, and raise children with your brother's widows, so the line goes on. She isn't asking lightly; in the world of the poem, a line with no sons means no one to make the offerings for the dead. But Bhishma says no. He reminds her what he swore, and why. Then he says, in effect: he could give up the three worlds, the kingdom of the gods, anything greater still, but he will not give up truth. The earth might lose its scent, water its wetness, the sun its glory, before he breaks his word. She asks once more, and he still holds. Here's the teaching. In Sanskrit, truth is satya, and Hindu tradition sets it near the heart of dharma. Many teachers put it this way: a promise is truth spoken ahead of time, so breaking it is a kind of lie. An Upanishad says it in three words, satyameva jayate, truth alone wins, and modern India took the line as its national motto. In Hindi, an unbreakable vow is still called a Bhishma pratigya, a vow like Bhishma's. But the poem is honest: the vow that made Satyavati queen now stands between her and an heir. Some readers see the picture of keeping your word at any cost; some see the first sign it will cost his family dearly. And Satyavati still has one thing she hasn't told anyone.
screen: `TAKE THE THRONE, SHE ASKS.` · `BHISHMA SAYS NO.` · `I WILL NOT GIVE UP TRUTH.` · `SATYAMEVA JAYATE.` · then, large: `A WORD GIVEN IS SACRED.`

segments.voice: Before a puja, many Hindus make a sankalpa: a stated intention, often with a little water in the palm. Hold your palm open. Make one small promise you can truly keep today: a call you'll return, a kind word you owe. Say it quietly, to God if you pray, or to yourself. Close your hand. Then keep it, today, the way Bhishma kept his.
Satyavati. The queen who asks Bhishma to break the vow that made her queen, and hears him choose truth.
Your line: satya, a word given is sacred. Tomorrow, Satyavati tells her secret. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: your cousin calls a promise he won't break 'a Bhishma pratigya'. what does he mean?
options: a vow kept like Bhishma's, even when it costs, because a given word is satya.
a promise only an old man can make.

fork.reveal: even when the queen herself begged, Bhishma would not give up truth. Hindi still names an iron vow after him.

Bhishma.meaning: Shantanu's son, who vowed never to take the throne

Satyavati.meaning: the fisherman's daughter who became queen mother of the Kurus

satyameva jayate.meaning: truth alone wins: an Upanishad's words, India's motto
